parts.name: joel-photon
parts.text: The suttas repeatedly call nibbāna unestablished or unsupported. Ud 8.1 says nibbāna has no coming, going, standing, passing, or arising. And then in SN 12.38 and SN 22.53 unestablishing consciousness is what ends renewed existence. Serendipitously, SN 12.64 uses the image of a beam of light that has nowhere to land to describe such unestablished consciousness. And most of us learned in physics 101 that photons don’t seem to have one definitive state until they are pinned down by measurement. So now we start to understand that saṃsāra is like that photon, the unestablished flows becoming established or pinned down by interrelating with other flows until they seem to be a solid world.

parts.name: joel-1
parts.text: MN 137 gives a two-step recipe. First you use unification (which I’d explain as collecting the mental processes into one attentional direction) to let go of diversity (distraction of the mental processes). Then you use non-identification (not taking anything to be “me”) to let go of unity too. In MN 121, at every depth of unification, the meditator checks what disturbance is still left, and tellingly, what they ultimately find is “just this much – that which depends on oneness.”

parts.name: plain-2
parts.text: Everything is happening according to natural laws, but we don’t live as those laws themselves. We live as a made-up abstraction built out of them, the unified sense of self. Because that’s what we are right now, pain, unsatisfactoriness, and injustice still hurt and still call for a response. But once you can touch ultimate reality (that already-perfect nature) for yourself, and see the path out of the illusory cycle of saṃsāra, those problems stop having the same ultimate psychological power over you.

parts.name: joel-3
parts.text: Even after the little king or queen fantasy disappears, the mind scurries into a subtler place: “Fine, then I must be the awareness that makes everything real.” But that’s just pushing the problem of what is real further down the lane. Now there’s something being labeled as awareness, which for some reason is more real than something else, even though the awareness needs the thing it’s aware of in order to call itself awareness. And those folks call themselves “non-dualists” in the sense of monism, everything is One (Advaita Vedanta). Clearly, that kind of non-duality is an oxymoron, false on the face of it (like my dad’s favorite oxymoron: “military intelligence”). What I find instead, and what I believe the Buddha was pointing to, are aware energy flows and the processes that gather them into a self & world.

parts.name: joel-4
parts.text: Iti 44 also shows the limit of nibbāna while you’re alive: a living arahant still has preferences and still feels pleasure and pain, although they won’t be reborn again, since there’s no more craving for existence driving that. So there’s no more rebirth ahead, that’s a relief. Yet except while in the nibbāna meditation itself, their constructed functioning that can feel pleasure and pain is still running. So in this article, “saṃsāric” refers to that constructed functioning itself, since it is what’s capable of dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness).

parts.name: plain-5
parts.text: That missing plural matters. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu opens correctly in The Mind Like Fire Unbound and The Wings to Awakening, saying the mind fabricates the experienced cosmos, including time and the present. But then he still leaves in one copy-pasted line in the singular, “consciousness without feature, without end, luminous all around,” which makes it sound like one single consciousness. He can’t imagine parallel flows as nibbāna, because the suttas say nibbāna lacks “differentiation.”

parts.name: joel-6
parts.text: Exactly: saṃsāra and nibbāna are the same light flows, which aren’t built from parts (uncompounded), seen two ways. It’s saṃsāra when those flows get tangled up as one world with a body in it that is made of matter that changes in time from moment to moment. It’s nibbāna when that tangling untangles/unweaves or never tangled to begin with.

parts.name: joel-7
parts.text: Nothing finds footing, because no assembled body-and-world has been set up for anything to stand on, and that’s the same reason suffering has nowhere to land (nor anywhere to sprout from). Light can be perceived as the material world, but it isn’t one of the objects in that world.

parts.name: joel-10
parts.text: Physics can’t show this from the outside, but meditation can show it from the inside: light sees itself. Suppose light buys a mirror from the local mirror shop, and starts admiring its own beauty. That’s like consciousness turning back on itself, and that turning-back is what begins to set up a mind (a “me” doing the watching). Reminds me of the Greek myth of Narcissus, who stared at his own beautiful reflection in a pond so long that he starved to death.
